narrative.text: A list of abbreviations and acronyms used in the 2021 HIV guideline update.

Defines key terms used in the 2021 HIV guidelines, starting with HIV types and acute infection. It sets age-group definitions for adults, adolescents, children and infants, and defines key and vulnerable populations. Further definitions cover terms such as serodiscordant couples and partners.

Acknowledges the many contributors to the guideline, starting with the GRADE methodologist and the co-chairs and members of the Clinical Guideline Development Group from many countries. It goes on to name other reviewers, partners and WHO staff. It ends by naming PEPFAR, the US CDC, USAID, Unitaid and the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation as funders.

The executive summary identifies the audience as national HIV programme managers, people living with HIV, health-care providers and policy-makers in low- and middle-income countries. It explains that the update followed WHO Guidelines Review Committee procedures and the GRADE approach. It sets out the public health rationale and introduces a summary table of the new recommendations, the revised monitoring algorithm and clinical considerations for rapid ART initiation.

Gives the epidemiological background, citing 38 million people living with HIV and 1.7 million new infections in 2019, with rising incidence in eastern Europe, central Asia and other regions. It notes that the 2020 Fast-Track targets were missed despite falling AIDS deaths. It then explains why updated guidance was needed on prevention, infant diagnosis, viral load monitoring and timing of ART for people with TB symptoms.
States that the guidelines aim to contribute to WHO's 13th General Programme of Work and the goal of ending AIDS by 2030.
Lists the target audience of the guidelines, chiefly national HIV programme managers and policy-makers, as well as clinicians, laboratory managers, community organizations and funding agencies.

Lists the guiding principles behind the guidelines, such as a public health approach to scaling up antiretroviral drugs and the involvement of people living with HIV. Others include strengthening wider health systems, protecting human rights and gender equity, and adapting to local context.

Summarises the methods used to develop the guideline, which links to earlier WHO HIV guidelines and followed Guidelines Review Committee procedures and GRADE. It describes how declarations of interest were managed and how systematic reviews and evidence-to-decision tables informed the recommendations.
A reference list for the introduction, citing UNAIDS data, UN political declarations and earlier WHO HIV guidelines.
A section divider heading for the clinical guidelines on antiretroviral drugs for HIV prevention.

Presents the conditional recommendation that the dapivirine vaginal ring may be offered as an extra prevention choice for women at substantial HIV risk. It gives background on oral PrEP uptake since 2015 and describes the ring as a female-initiated silicone device releasing an NNRTI, and it notes that long-acting injectable cabotegravir was not yet assessed.

Defines substantial HIV risk as incidence above 3 per 100 person-years without PrEP and discusses how thresholds and risk assessment tools may vary. The section then covers evidence and considerations for the dapivirine vaginal ring, as the start and end of this cut block indicate. Its closing part discusses switching between or combining the ring and oral PrEP, the need for adherence, and unknowns about whether the ring adds new users or replaces oral PrEP. It ends with cost and cost-effectiveness, calling for further analysis using real-world data.
A reference list for the dapivirine vaginal ring section, citing PrEP trials, regulatory reviews and studies of ring use, acceptability and adherence among African women.
A section divider heading for the clinical guidelines on diagnostics and treatment monitoring.

Presents the strong recommendation to use point-of-care nucleic acid testing to diagnose HIV in infants and children under 18 months. It explains the need, citing low early infant testing coverage, long laboratory turnaround times and high mortality among untreated infants. The later part of this cut block covers implementation, such as integrating point-of-care tools into laboratory networks, training and same-day linkage to care. It ends with research gaps, including quality assurance and a possible dual-use test for diagnosis and viral load.

Presents the conditional recommendation that point-of-care viral load testing may be used to monitor people receiving ART. It describes the growth of viral load testing since 2016 and remaining barriers, and introduces new point-of-care technologies giving results within one to two hours. Implementation considerations include fitting the technology within the treatment monitoring algorithm, integrated laboratory networks and setting patient priorities given limited capacity. It notes that rapid results may help prevent drug resistance, especially in children and adolescents.

Box 2 lists priority groups for point-of-care viral load testing, such as pregnant and breastfeeding women, children and people with suspected treatment failure, and stresses training, quality assurance and treatment literacy. It ends with research gaps on optimizing implementation and a single test for diagnosis and viral load.

Explains the updated treatment monitoring algorithm in WHO's HIV guidance, noting that rapid ART initiation, the move from efavirenz-based regimens to dolutegravir and rising pretreatment NNRTI resistance have changed the context since the 2016 viral load algorithm. It reviews four questions: when to do the first viral load test, when to repeat it after an elevated result, whether to switch NNRTI-based regimens after a single test, and what threshold defines treatment failure. Supporting evidence is set out for each consideration. The section ends with research gaps, including the clinical relevance of low-level viraemia on dolutegravir and monitoring needs for children, adolescents and pregnant and breastfeeding women.

Box 3 sets out implementation considerations for viral load monitoring in pregnant and breastfeeding women, such as prioritizing same-day point-of-care testing and adherence counselling at every antenatal and postnatal visit. It specifies when to test according to the timing of ART initiation and what to do, including enhanced infant prophylaxis and infant testing, when viral load exceeds 1000 copies/ml.

A list of references for the chapters on infant diagnosis and treatment monitoring, citing mainly UNAIDS data, WHO guidelines and studies on point-of-care infant diagnosis and viral load testing, including dried blood spot samples.
A section heading for chapter 4 on clinical guidelines for the timing of antiretroviral therapy.

Gives the recommendation that people living with HIV start ART as soon as possible within two weeks of starting TB treatment, whatever their CD4 count, except where meningitis is present. The background traces earlier WHO advice on ART timing during TB treatment and notes the lack of alignment with rapid ART guidance. Evidence summarized includes trials showing that immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome was not more frequent with dolutegravir or raltegravir than with efavirenz.

Box 4 explains that ART should be delayed in people with cryptococcal or TB meningitis, for 4–6 weeks and at least four weeks respectively, because early treatment raises adverse events and mortality. The section then extends the earlier-ART recommendation to children by extrapolation from adult evidence, given the high risks of delay in young children. It closes with research gaps on newer ARVs in TB coinfection, corticosteroids to prevent immune reconstitution syndrome and multi-disease adherence support.
A list of references for the section on ART timing in people with TB, citing WHO TB and HIV guidelines and trials of early versus delayed ART during TB treatment.

Reports that a systematic review on TB symptom criteria for same-day ART initiation found no studies directly addressing the question, so the Guideline Development Group chose to clarify clinical considerations rather than make a new recommendation.

Box 5 revises rapid ART guidance so that people with signs of TB, other than meningitis, start ART while TB is rapidly investigated, with follow-up within seven days, whereas ART is delayed if TB or cryptococcal meningitis is suspected. The background notes that TB caused 30% of HIV-associated deaths in 2019 and that rapid ART initiation has been recommended since 2017. Research gaps include the effect of this approach on care outcomes and the role of prophylactic corticosteroids in preventing immune reconstitution syndrome.
A reference list for the rapid ART section, followed by short sections on how WHO will monitor uptake of the guidelines, potential barriers, and modular updating of the guidance.
A section heading for disseminating, adapting and implementing the guidelines, with web links to a mobile app.

Annex 1 describes the background to developing this clinical guideline, explaining that it updates the 2016 consolidated ARV guidelines in a modular way. Table A1 maps guidance issued since 2016 to the chapters of the consolidated guidelines, and a figure shows the hub-and-spoke model of technical scoping meetings. It notes the new recommendations will be integrated into the 2021 consolidated guidelines.

Table A2 lists technical scoping meetings held between 2017 and 2020 that informed the guideline update, and the text describes the virtual Guideline Development Group meeting held in late 2020 because of COVID-19. It explains how seven systematic reviews and other evidence were summarized and rated using GRADE.

Table A3 summarizes the methods of the systematic reviews behind each PICO question, including the dapivirine vaginal ring, point-of-care infant diagnosis and point-of-care viral load monitoring, with review leads, search dates and included studies. The text then describes how the virtual meeting was run, with a 60% voting threshold agreed but all recommendations reached by consensus. Evidence-to-decision tables were prepared in line with GRADE and discussed with a methodologist.

Table A4 defines the criteria used in evidence-to-decision tables, such as certainty of evidence, benefits and risks, values, costs, equity and acceptability. The text then describes how conflicts of interest of the External Review Group were managed and how the draft guidelines were peer reviewed in November 2020.

Annex 2 presents a simplified algorithm for diagnosing HIV in exposed infants and children under 18 months, with key principles such as testing the mother, NAT at nine months and confirming any positive result. Notes explain birth testing, point-of-care NAT and retesting to avoid false positives, and the page ends with WHO HIV department contact details.

The title, copyright and licence pages and table of contents of WHO's March 2021 updated recommendations on HIV prevention, infant diagnosis, antiretroviral initiation and monitoring, with ISBNs. The contents list the chapters, annexes, tables and figures, including the PICO questions and technical scoping meetings. It also gives the suggested citation and standard WHO disclaimers.
